options.consequence: The organisation treats the exercise result as actionable evidence. Leadership understands exposure, interim measures reduce near-term impact, and remediation is prioritised with owners and deadlines. A follow-up technical test verifies whether objectives become achievable.

options.text: Update the plan document to state an 18-hour RTO so it matches the exercise result, without remediation.
options.consequence: Documentation aligns with failure, but customer and business impact remain unacceptable. The underlying resilience gap persists and governance may wrongly assume risk was managed because paperwork changed.
options.whyWeaker: Changing objectives without business agreement and remediation avoids the problem rather than solving it. A stronger response addresses capability, ownership and informed decision-making.

options.text: Treat the tabletop as theoretical and take no action because a real outage has not occurred.
options.consequence: Known recoverability weaknesses remain unaddressed until a real incident causes extended disruption. The value of exercising is lost and confidence in continuity reporting is undermined.
options.whyWeaker: Exercises exist to reveal gaps safely. A stronger response uses findings to improve readiness before a live incident tests them under pressure.

options.text: Immediately purchase additional backup tooling without analysing dependencies, priorities or recovery procedures.
options.consequence: Spending may not close the largest bottlenecks, such as dependency rebuild time or unclear procedures. Improvements remain unproven and the RTO/RPO gap may persist despite new tooling.
options.whyWeaker: Tooling can help, but effective recovery requires understanding failure modes, dependencies and tested procedures. A stronger response combines analysis, prioritised remediation and validation.

items.bestPractice: When exercises show RTO/RPO gaps, escalate transparently, analyse root causes and dependencies, implement prioritised remediation with interim controls, and validate through technical tests. Keep plans current with architecture changes and ensure objectives are agreed with business owners.
items.managementGuidance: Continuity maturity is measured by recoverability, not by having documents. Treat failed objectives as risk signals requiring ownership, funding decisions and retesting.

stakeholderViews.Platform owner: Needs clear priorities and support to close recovery gaps.
stakeholderViews.Operations lead: Concerned about customer impact during prolonged outages.
stakeholderViews.Risk manager: Wants documented treatment and validation timeline.

items.title: Audit requests evidence for a key control but logs are unavailable
items.context: During an internal audit of change management, auditors request evidence that emergency production changes in the last quarter were reviewed and approved retrospectively. The system team reports that relevant application logs were not retained due to a misconfigured retention setting, and approval emails are scattered across personal inboxes. The control owner believes the changes were appropriate but cannot readily produce consistent evidence.
items.situation: Decide how to handle the missing evidence and the underlying control issue identified during the audit.
informationAvailable: Auditors requested evidence of retrospective review and approval for emergency production changes in the last quarter.
Application logs for the period are unavailable due to retention misconfiguration; approval records are incomplete and decentralised.
Control owner asserts changes were appropriate but cannot provide consistent, retrievable evidence.
Ambiguity: it is not yet known how many emergency changes occurred or whether any introduced security or operational issues.
Change management policy requires documented approval, traceability and review for emergency changes.

options.text: Reconstruct available evidence transparently, assess the control as ineffective for the period where evidence is missing, investigate impact of emergency changes, and remediate logging and recordkeeping with defined ownership.
options.consequence: The audit conclusion is based on evidence rather than assurance alone. Potential impact is assessed, and corrective actions address retention, centralised records and monitoring so future audits can verify control operation. Credibility with auditors is maintained.

options.text: Provide verbal assurance that changes were reviewed and ask auditors to close the finding without evidence.
options.consequence: The finding remains unresolved because assurance cannot substitute for evidence. Trust with audit stakeholders erodes, and the systemic logging weakness continues to expose the organisation in future reviews and incidents.
options.whyWeaker: Controls must be demonstrable. A stronger response acknowledges evidence gaps, evaluates impact and fixes the conditions that prevent proof of operation.

options.text: Recreate missing approvals now and backdate records to satisfy the audit request.
options.consequence: Fabricated or backdated records create integrity and misconduct risk far exceeding the original control gap. Audit and legal exposure increases significantly and governance credibility is damaged.
options.whyWeaker: Evidence integrity is non-negotiable. A stronger response reconstructs honestly, documents limitations and remediates rather than falsifying records.

options.text: Disable emergency changes entirely to avoid future evidence problems.
options.consequence: Operational resilience suffers because legitimate urgent fixes may be blocked. The organisation avoids evidence issues by restricting necessary capability rather than improving traceability and review.
options.whyWeaker: Emergency change is a valid process when governed. A stronger response preserves capability with reliable logging, approvals and retrospective review evidence.

items.bestPractice: Auditability requires reliable, retrievable evidence. When evidence is missing, be transparent about limitations, assess control effectiveness and impact, and remediate root causes such as retention, workflow design and ownership. Never fabricate records.
items.managementGuidance: A missing log is often a control design failure, not just an audit inconvenience. Fix evidence generation at source so compliance and incident investigation both improve.

stakeholderViews.Control owner: Believes intent was met but lacks records.
stakeholderViews.Internal auditor: Needs sufficient, reliable evidence to conclude.
stakeholderViews.IT operations: Can correct retention and workflow gaps.

items.title: Urgent request for policy exception to allow remote administrative access
items.context: A critical outage requires vendor support outside business hours. The vendor asks for direct remote administrative access from an unmanaged device because their managed laptop is unavailable. The request bypasses standard remote access controls (MFA enforcement, device compliance, jump host and session recording). Service restoration is urgent, but the affected system processes sensitive operational data.
items.situation: Decide how to handle the urgent request for remote administrative access that conflicts with security policy.
informationAvailable: Vendor requests direct remote admin access from an unmanaged device during a critical outage.
Standard controls require MFA, compliant device, jump host/brokered access and session recording for privileged remote access.
Affected system processes sensitive operational data; restoration is time-critical.
Ambiguity: it is unclear how long restoration will take and whether an alternative managed access path can be arranged quickly.
No pre-approved emergency access procedure is documented for third-party administrators.

options.text: Use a controlled emergency path: grant least-privilege, time-limited access through an approved broker or jump mechanism where possible, enforce strong authentication and logging, document a formal exception with compensating controls, and review immediately after restoration.
options.consequence: Urgent support proceeds with reduced exposure and clear accountability. Compensating controls and time limits constrain risk, actions are traceable, and the exception informs improvement of emergency access procedures.

options.text: Grant full unrestricted access immediately from the unmanaged device to minimise downtime, with no additional conditions.
options.consequence: Sensitive systems are exposed to elevated compromise risk with weak traceability. If misuse or malware occurs, the organisation cannot demonstrate due care or control over privileged access during an emergency.
options.whyWeaker: Urgency does not remove the need for proportionate controls. A stronger response enables recovery while preserving least privilege, monitoring and accountability.

options.text: Refuse all support until the vendor returns with a fully compliant device, regardless of outage impact.
options.consequence: Outage duration may increase significantly, causing avoidable business harm. A rigid stance without contingency planning can reduce trust in security as an enabler of safe operations.
options.whyWeaker: A stronger response seeks secure alternatives and governed exceptions. Policy should protect the organisation while enabling controlled incident response.

options.text: Share internal admin credentials over a call so the vendor can work indirectly, avoiding remote access tooling.
options.consequence: Credential confidentiality and attribution are lost, creating serious security and audit issues. Actions cannot be reliably tied to an individual and credential recovery becomes urgent after the incident.
options.whyWeaker: Sharing credentials undermines identity, accountability and security. A stronger response uses attributable, monitored access even under emergency conditions.

items.bestPractice: Emergency access should be possible but governed: least privilege, time-bound approval, strong authentication, monitoring/logging and documented compensating controls. Prefer brokered access and avoid unmanaged endpoints or shared credentials.
items.managementGuidance: Define emergency privileged access before crises occur. In the moment, balance availability with containment and traceability so urgent fixes do not create lasting exposure.

stakeholderViews.Vendor manager: Must ensure third-party access meets policy conditions.

items.title: Conflicting regulatory expectations across jurisdictions for data handling
items.context: Vanguard is expanding a customer service platform to two jurisdictions. Local guidance in Jurisdiction A emphasises rapid incident reporting and broad cooperation with supervisory requests, while Jurisdiction B imposes stricter limits on cross-border data transfer and requires specific contractual safeguards. Current platform logging and support workflows route tickets and diagnostic data through a central region by default. Legal, compliance and engineering disagree on whether to delay launch or implement interim controls.
items.situation: Determine how to proceed with the platform expansion given conflicting cross-jurisdictional regulatory requirements.
informationAvailable: Jurisdiction A expects rapid incident reporting and cooperation; Jurisdiction B restricts cross-border transfers and requires specific safeguards.
Current support and logging workflows route data through a central region by default, potentially conflicting with Jurisdiction B constraints.
Legal and compliance interpretations differ on permissible interim measures; engineering estimates significant effort to re-architect data flows.
Ambiguity: the exact categories of personal and operational data in tickets/logs and their transfer paths are not fully mapped.
Launch delay has commercial impact, but non-compliance could trigger enforcement, remediation orders and contractual issues.

options.text: Map data flows and obligations by jurisdiction, implement feasible interim controls (minimisation, regional routing, access restrictions, contractual safeguards) where compliant, and phase launch or delay high-risk elements until requirements can be demonstrably met.
options.consequence: Decisions are based on evidence about data, transfers and obligations. The organisation reduces exposure through targeted controls and avoids launching non-compliant processing. Stakeholders receive a clear, defensible rationale for sequencing and investment.

options.text: Launch globally now and address jurisdiction-specific requirements after customer onboarding scales.
options.consequence: Potential unlawful transfers or inadequate safeguards may occur from day one, creating regulatory and remediation risk that is costly to unwind. Post-hoc fixes are harder once data and processes are live.
options.whyWeaker: Cross-border and regulatory obligations must shape design before processing. A stronger response aligns architecture and controls to known requirements prior to launch.

options.text: Apply the strictest interpretation everywhere without assessing applicability, data categories or business impact.
options.consequence: Some risks are reduced, but unnecessary constraints may harm service quality and delay value without clear legal necessity. Resources may be misallocated if actual data flows do not warrant all measures.
options.whyWeaker: A risk- and evidence-based approach targets controls to real obligations and data realities. A stronger response avoids both under- and over-compliance driven by assumption.

options.text: Delegate the decision entirely to engineering to choose the fastest technical option.
options.consequence: Legal and compliance obligations may be overlooked, and accountability for regulatory risk becomes unclear. Technical speed does not ensure lawful processing or defensible governance.
options.whyWeaker: Regulatory decisions require cross-functional ownership. A stronger response integrates legal interpretation, compliance assessment and engineering feasibility into a documented decision.

items.bestPractice: Manage multi-jurisdiction compliance by mapping data flows and obligations, identifying conflicts, applying defensible interim safeguards, and sequencing launch decisions based on demonstrable compliance. Document assumptions, decisions and residual risks.
items.managementGuidance: When regulations pull in different directions, clarity comes from data mapping and accountable trade-offs. Do not guess at compliance or treat legal requirements as purely technical constraints.

stakeholderViews.Legal counsel: Focused on enforceable obligations and defensibility.
stakeholderViews.Engineering manager: Concerned about rework and delivery timelines.
